extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, picture editors, journalism professionals and readers interested in news photography ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and argumentative criteria for evaluating digital alterations in documentary/photojournalistic images, and for forming codes of ethics about image manipulation in news photography. Focuses on what kinds of edits deceive the public versus acceptable aesthetic enhancements, plus related institutional responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPPA Code: do not alter content that deceives the public
rubrics_metrics.description: "In documentary photojournalism, it is wrong to alter the content of a photograph in any way (electronically, or in the darkroom) that deceives the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the explicit standard cited by NCPPA board members; it establishes the high-level prohibition that manipulations which change factual content or mislead viewers are unethical. Use this as a baseline test: does the alteration change what actually happened or how a viewer would understand the scene?

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent to deceive vs aesthetic enhancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether a photographer "intended to deceive readers or contest judges" versus made aesthetic choices that did not aim at deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should consider the photographer's intent — e.g., The Observer concluded Schneider "did not intend to deceive" though he "went over the line" with some techniques. Intent matters when judging ethical culpability, though unintended misleading effects still merit discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alterations that change essential information vs purely aesthetic changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether edits alter the "fundamental information in the photographs" (content) or only their "esthetical value."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interpretation of the event, actions, or subjects would remain identical before and after editing, the change is aesthetic. Examples given: removing background elements (parking lots, fences, people) was argued as aesthetic not content-changing in Schneider's case. Judges should separate content-misleading edits from enhancements of mood, color, or composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on compositing/fabrication (creating a 'made-up picture')
rubrics_metrics.description: Edits that combine parts of multiple images or otherwise fabricate a scene (e.g., Brian Walski's compositing) constitute deception and are grounds for dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositing that creates events or relationships that did not occur is treated as serious misconduct. This is contrasted with single-image tonal/color adjustments or localized retouching that do not invent new factual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges must understand tools and aesthetics before condemning
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation panels should not mistake "aesthetically pleasing traits" or legitimate use of new tools for misinformation; lack of technical/aesthetic understanding is a lapse of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award panels and editors should be familiar with current digital techniques (burns, dodges, color enhancement) so they don't conflate standard image-making practice with deception. The author criticizes NCPPA for failing to appreciate what "the new tools of this century bring to photography."

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider printing/reproduction variability when judging edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some variations denounced as transformations may be ascribable to changes in printing quality or reproduction differences between publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before concluding an image was altered unethically, evaluators should account for how different presses, paper, and color reproduction can change appearance; minor differences don't necessarily indicate deceptive manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographer responsibility: define goals (veracity) not tool bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes of ethics should define photographer responsibilities in terms of the "Veracity in the story being told" rather than forbidding specific tools or techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues "The definition of a responsibility cannot [be] established by setting a constraint on the tools to be used" — instead, state the ethical goal (truthfulness) and let professionals choose appropriate methods to achieve that goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and evidence: release of raw files for audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing raw files and cooperating with audits (as The Observer released Schneider's raw files) is a means to assess whether edits were deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raw-file review can clarify whether alterations materially changed content or were limited to tonal/color/cleanup work. Transparency is a practical mechanism for resolving disputes about integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual integrity: captions, cropping, and editorial placement matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors' use of captions, crops, or placing images with arbitrary headers/text can mislead; editorial context can be as deceptive as image manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of truthfulness must include how images are used editorially. The piece accuses publications of using pictures "out of context to satisfy your editorial needs," indicating that responsibility for honesty extends beyond production to placement and captioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional practices and conflicts (embedded photojournalism) affect credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangements like embedded journalists with the military compromised information and created propaganda, so institutional contexts must be considered when judging integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing credibility and ethical breaches, consider larger institutional behaviors (e.g., embedded reporting, staged photo-ops) which may produce far greater distortions than small digital adjustments; don't scapegoat individual photographers for systemic failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not selectively punish tool use while ignoring larger manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: It's inconsistent to condemn photographers for using digital tools for aesthetic improvement while tolerating organizational propaganda, staged photo-ops, or other manipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical enforcement should be consistent across types of manipulation; the author argues that focusing on Photoshop dodging/burning distracts from more serious forms of misinformation perpetrated by publishers or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel decisions should weigh likelihood of public misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those edits that have a "slightest possibility of being misinterpreted" as to their content should be considered deceptive; trivial aesthetic changes that do not create plausible misinterpretations should not be grounds for award rescission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reasonable viewers would understand the scene differently after the edit. If interpretation remains "absolutely identical," punitive measures are inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical enforcement requires imagination and clear definitions, not infantilizing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes that simply tell photographers what tools they can't use are inadequate; rules should be imaginative, clear about goals, and treat photographers as responsible professionals rather than children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges moving away from prescriptive 'do not use X tool' rules toward goal-oriented standards emphasizing responsibility and veracity, allowing professionals to exercise judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors/newspapers bear responsibility for overall accuracy and should be held accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the "newspaper organizations and associations" share blame for false arguments and misleading information and should be held responsible rather than only photographers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical assessment should include institutional accountability (editorial choices, fact-checking, staging, and messaging), not only technical image manipulation by individual photographers.
